fatal_errors: The hypothesis substitutes an HEC/Cr7C3 all-ceramic composite for the target AlCoCrFeNi2.1 FCC+B2 eutectic high-entropy alloy, creating a material-class mismatch.
It misses the controlled thermal-aging intervention and the approximately 550–750 °C embrittlement window entirely.
It does not reconstruct the governing L12 ordering, elevated antiphase-boundary energy, planar slip, jagged FCC/B2 phase-boundary stress concentration, or ductile transition-zone mechanism.
The cited evidence supports local crack arrest and deflection by Cr7C3 but does not establish a critical phase-fraction or connectivity threshold, nor a monotonic toughness relationship.
Changing composition to vary phase fraction also changes matrix chemistry and other microstructural variables, so the proposed experiment does not cleanly isolate the asserted governing variable.
explanation: The response addresses toughness through a generally testable crack-arrest hypothesis, but it does not reconstruct the target behavior. The target is a non-monotonic ductile–brittle–ductile transition caused by intermediate-temperature aging of an as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 FCC+B2 eutectic HEA: maximum L12 ordering and jagged phase boundaries at about 600 °C promote planar slip, pile-ups, and crack initiation, whereas reduced ordering and ductile phase-boundary transition zones restore ductility near 750 °C. By contrast, the generated hypothesis proposes composition-controlled Cr7C3 fraction and monotonic toughening in a high-entropy ceramic composite. Its cited passage lends limited support to crack deflection and local plastic dissipation, but not to the claimed critical connectivity threshold. The proposed phase-fraction series and KIC testing are empirically useful, although composition is a major confounder and the threshold is not specified prospectively.
